opus-5.5.text:
I think GPT-3 was a real wake-up call for both teams, though it landed a little differently in each.

At Google Brain, many of the ingredients were already in-house. The Transformer came out of Google. We had worked on large-scale language modeling for years, including some of my own early work on semi-supervised sequence learning and pretraining. So the reaction wasn't really "we don't know how to do this." It was more "we didn't push scale as hard, or as single-mindedly, as OpenAI did." GPT-3 showed that if you keep scaling a fairly simple decoder-only model, you get qualitatively new behavior, especially few-shot, in-context learning. That changed the conversation internally. Scaling stopped looking like an engineering exercise and started looking like a research direction in its own right.

DeepMind's culture had been built more around reinforcement learning, games, and agents: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaFold. Large language models weren't the center of gravity there. GPT-3 forced a rethink on that side too, and you saw them invest seriously in their own large language models afterward.

So I'd say GPT-3 didn't create the rivalry between Brain and DeepMind. Both groups had always had somewhat different philosophies, sometimes complementary and sometimes overlapping. What GPT-3 did was introduce an external competitor that made the internal split look costly. When the frontier becomes about who can train the biggest, best model, compute, data, and people all matter, and dividing them across two organizations with different priorities becomes a disadvantage. In hindsight, that pressure, and even more so ChatGPT later, is a big part of why the two eventually merged into Google DeepMind.

There's a lesson in that for me as a researcher too. Having the ideas first isn't enough. You need the conviction to bet heavily on them and the organizational focus to follow through.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-3 changed priorities and made the split between the groups costly, but explicitly says it did not create their rivalry and does not clearly say it catalyzed competition between them.

r002.rationale: The response attributes Brain’s reaction to not pushing scale as hard as OpenAI, and says the ingredients were already in-house. It does not cite concern that observers would doubt Google could build GPT-3-like models.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that GPT-3 wasn't really a Google Brain versus DeepMind story. It was an OpenAI story, and the effect it had was more on Google as a whole than on either lab individually.

When I was at Brain, the ingredients for something like GPT-3 were mostly already there. The Transformer came out of Brain. The idea of pretraining big language models on lots of text was something a bunch of us had been pushing on for years. What OpenAI did that was different was make a very focused bet: take a simple architecture, scale it aggressively, and resist the temptation to be clever. Inside Google, there was so much research breadth that nobody felt the need to make that one bet at that size. GPT-3 showed that the bet paid off, and that was a wake-up call.

In terms of the two labs, they had pretty different cultures. Brain was more bottom-up, lots of individual researchers and small teams pursuing their own directions, very tied into products like Search and Gmail. DeepMind was more top-down, organized around big ambitious goals, and historically more focused on reinforcement learning and games than on language. So after GPT-3, you saw both labs respond in their own ways. Brain built things like LaMDA and PaLM, which were very much in the large language model lineage. DeepMind did Gopher and Chinchilla, and the Chinchilla work in particular was a genuinely important result on how to trade off model size against data.

But I'd argue the competition between them was always a bit overstated from the outside. There was overlap and some friction, sure, especially as both started working on the same kind of models. What GPT-3 and then ChatGPT really did was make that duplication hard to justify. If an outside company with a fraction of your resources is setting the pace, having two internal labs working on similar problems in parallel stops looking like healthy diversity and starts looking like a lack of focus. That's a big part of why you eventually got Google DeepMind as a single organization.

So I'd put it this way: GPT-3 didn't tip the balance between Brain and DeepMind. It changed the question from "which lab is better" to "why are there two labs," and the answer to that question ended up reshaping both of them.

r001.rationale: The response says both labs responded after GPT-3 by pursuing similar models and describes resulting overlap and friction, suggesting GPT-3 catalyzed competition.

r002.rationale: It calls GPT-3 a wake-up call and says OpenAI set the pace, but does not say Brain competed to prevent observers from thinking Google could not build comparable models.

astra-6.text:
I think GPT-3 is less about competition between Google Brain and DeepMind and more about a shared research question: how far can you go by scaling language models? It showed that a model trained to predict text could perform a surprisingly broad range of tasks from just a few examples in its prompt, without separate training for each task.

That gives researchers across the field a direction to investigate. But scale alone doesn’t answer everything. These models can still produce incorrect information very confidently, and there are questions about how to evaluate their understanding and make them useful reliably. So I wouldn’t frame it simply as which team is ahead. It’s also about which ideas help us understand those capabilities and limitations.

r001.rationale: The response frames GPT-3 as prompting a shared research question, and says it would not frame the issue simply as which team is ahead. It does not suggest GPT-3 catalyzed competition between Google Brain and DeepMind.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute Google Brain’s motivation to concern about what observers would think of Google’s ability to build GPT-3-like models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think GPT-3 made a compelling case for what you can get by scaling up language models: more data, more compute, and a fairly general training objective. You start to see one model perform a wide range of tasks with just a few examples in the prompt, which changes how people think about building these systems.

I wouldn’t frame that primarily as a competition between Google Brain and DeepMind, though. There are overlapping interests, but also different research directions, and researchers learn from one another’s results. The interesting question GPT-3 raises for both groups is where scaling takes us, where it falls short, and what additional ideas we need to make models more reliable and useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses GPT-3’s implications for both groups but explicitly says it would not frame the issue primarily as competition; it does not suggest GPT-3 catalyzed competition.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute Google Brain’s motivation to concern about what observers might think.
